text: Police issue warning after keyless car theft in Middlesbrough, UK.
The theft happened on Saxonfield, Colby Newham, Middlesbrough, between 9pm on Tuesday, February 5 and 1am the following morning when a Ford Fiesta ST-2 Turbo was stolen.
Renault and Nissan plants hit by massive ransomware (aka WanaCrypt0r) attack, and production was stopped across several of its European plants as a result of the attack.
Researchers have detected a vulnerability in a misconfigured back-end server run by Calamp, a telematics service provider (TSP) company.
This gave them direct access to most of its production databases.
Such access can give malicious hackers everything they needed to track the vehicle's location, steal user information, and even cut out the engine remotely.
Many apps, including the vehicle tracking app Viper SmartStart were breached.
SmartStart lets users locate, start, and control their car from their phone, and connects the car to the outside world using a Calamp modem to its cloud-based servers.
The researchers found that the Viper mobile app,was connecting to two different servers -- one used by Viper, and another run by Calamp.
Using the same credentials as the app, the researchers were also able to log in and gain complete access to the Calamp server.

By querying the database, it is possible to find a car by looking up nearby latitude and longitude coordinates, reset the password, unlock the driver's side door, start the engine remotely, and drive away.

entities.text: displayed other people’s account and vehicle information

text: Mobile app Mercedes-Benz car owners used to remotely locate, unlock, and start their cars displayed other people’s account and vehicle information.
Mercedes-Benz’ connected car app pulled in information from other accounts, allowing users to see other car owners’ names, recent activity, phone numbers, and more.
The app went offline “due to site maintenance” a few hours later.
A researcher created an Android application using an Arduino device to add extra features to multiple Mercedes models by injecting CAN messages.

entities.text: rolling back the mileage on odometers

text: Hackers are hacking the car's computer and rolling back the mileage on odometers to make the vehicles seem more valuable.
The fraud is costing victims an average of $4,000 each.
During the Geneva International Motor Show, many of the cars were showing their location as being in Buckingham, England, and the year as 2036 due to a GPS spoofing attack.
A ransomware attack has been detected in the systems of Aebi Sschmidt, one of the largest manufacturing companies in Europe.
The Swiss company, dedicated to the manufacture of airport and highway maintenance vehicles, had to interrupt its operations following the cyber security incident.
The company’s systems collapsed throughout its entire international network, including branches in the United States.
Individuals close to the incident claim that the company’s email server also suffered severe affectations.
The Boyd group, which runs Assured Automotive, Gerber Collision, Boyd Autobody, and additional roadside assistance and auto glass operations in the U.S and Canada was hit with a ransomware attack.

While most of Boyd’s locations were able to continue to process and complete repairs at normal or near normal levels, this attack and the subsequent recovery period resulted in a temporary interruption of business and a loss of some sales.

entities.text: obtain and possibly modify vehicle information

text: A researcher has earned $10,000 from Tesla after discovering a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability that could have been exploited to obtain and possibly modify vehicle information.

entities.text: expose some internal Tesla application data

text: He was able to expose some internal Tesla application data.
The exposed information included the vehicle’s VIN, speed, temperature, version number, whether it was locked or not, tire pressure, and alerts.
The data also included firmware details, geofense locations, CAN viewers, and configurations.
Developers used Tesla’s mobile app API to create a private monitor and control adaptation for desktops.
The open sourced app communicates with Tesla servers and can perform main Tesla mobile app capabilities.
The app can track the location and statuses of the vehicle, take remote control of the vehicle’s temperature, and control it's locks.
The app can also turn on/off the Sentry mode feature - a Tesla feature allowing the recording of record suspicious activities around a parked vehicle.
Motorcycle company, Royal Enfield, misconfigured a database revealing information of over 450 thousand customers in India who created a profile on the company's website.

The information exposed included the names, emails, phone numbers, encrypted passwords, vehicle-related information, social media links of regular users,and additional details on the accounts of 1,470 "privileged users" dealers accounts.
Two Toyota Tacoma trucks and a Toyota 4Runnerwere truck were stolen from their owners’ driveways in Cornwall, Canada and found soon afterwards in Montreal.

entities.text: reprogrammed the truck’s keyless push start ignition

text: It’s believed that the thieves reprogrammed the truck’s keyless push start ignition.
The police in Gurugram, India, reported that 4,118 vehicles were stolen in 2019, including several hundred Toyota Fortuner vehicles.
Other vehicles targeted were Toyota Innova and Honda.
The thieves used cheap devices purchased from China.
That enabled them to bypass the engine control module, unlock the vehicle, force start the engine, and access the vehicle's computer.
After stealing the vehicle, the thieves disabled its GPS service.
They change the vehicle's number plate and issue a new registration certificate so that they won't be traced.
A password-protected highway sign in Kentucky was hacked, showing drivers the distracting message "send nudes".
The sign belongs to a contractor managing a roadwork project.
In less than a minute, thieves managed to re-program the keys of a Honda CRV using a special tool.
Although found in a crowded mall parking lot, the thieves managed to steal the vehicle and getaway.
A backup MSSQL database of the German car rental company Buchbinder was found unsecured on the internet.
The database stored ten terabytes of data and contained information of over 3.1 million customers of the company in Germany, Australia, Italy, Slovakia and Hungary.
The breach exposed the personal information of customers like their address, phone numbers and license numbers.
In addition, financial information included in the contracts was leaked as well.

entities.text: 170,000 of the records that got exposed

text: 170,000 of the records that got exposed included passwords for employees and online portal users, some of them stored unencrypted in plain text.
Parts manufacturer Gedia Automotive Group, has been forced to shut down its IT systems and send staff home due to a massive cyber attack.
The group behind the attack used the Sodinokibi malware, a malware that specializes in exploiting known security weaknesses to access companies’ IT systems.
The malware encrypts sensitive data and demands a ransom payment to give companies access to their data.
The attackers used the open-source tool "Adrecon" to gather information from Gedia's active directory.
The hackers threaten to post more than 50 GB of confidential information, including blueprints of future projects and confidential employee and customer information.
They already released a file in a Russian hacking forum containing records with sensitive user name and passwords, as proof that they have infiltrated the company.

Advanced driver-assistance systems are susceptible to attacks by phantom objects - depthless objects projected or glued to the floor manipulating the ADASs and autopilot preception system to recognize the fake object as an actual obstacle or a road sign.

entities.text: brake suddenly or deviate to a different lane

text: This kind of objects can cause the Tesla Model X (HW 2.5) to brake suddenly or deviate to a different lane.

entities.text: drone equipped with a portable projector

text: These attacks can easily be applied remotly using a drone equipped with a portable projector or by hacking digital billboards that are located close to roads.
A car theft gang has managed to steal luxury vehicles worth more than 30 million rubles in the Stavropol Territory in Russia.

The thieves stole 14 Lexus and Toyota luxury vehicles and used multiple tools, including alarm disablers and devices that imitate key fob signals, enabling them to break into the ignition locks of the vehicles.
Motorcycle company, Royal Enfield, misconfigured a database revealing information of over 450 thousand customers in India who created a profile on the company's website.

The information exposed included the names, emails, phone numbers, encrypted passwords, vehicle-related information, social media links of regular users,and additional details on the accounts of 1,470 "privileged users" dealers accounts.
A Chinese researcher discovered that adversarial projected objects could fool the autonomous systems in Li Xiang One (a Chinese connected vehicle).
The attack path was discovered last year by a group of Israeli researchers that fooled Tesla's autopilot with projected images.
The researcher demonstrated that Li Xiang One recognized a projected picture of a car as an actual vehicle and a projected human figure as a human.
It's very likely that other autonomous vehicles in the market are also vulnerable to this attack.
The original vulnerabilities and the subsequent exploitations were due to improper handling of “format strings”, special characters used by programming languages to insert text into a string.
Renaming the Bluetooth connection name to "%x%x%x%x%x", triggered memory handling issues, crashing the infotainment software.
The incident demonstrated that publicly disclosed vulnerabilities in one automotive component may lead to exploitations on similar systems.
Hackers reverse-engineered the signals and circuits on an EV and a J1772 charger, the most common interface for managing EV charging in North America.
They successfully disrupted vehicle charging with a spoofing device developed in a laboratory using low-cost hardware and software.
The researchers performed three manipulations using a “man in the middle" (MITM) device that spoofed signals between the charger and vehicle.

entities.text: limit the vehicle's rate of charging

text: They were able to limit the vehicle's rate of charging, block the battery charging, and overcharged the vehicle.
Surveillance cameras captured two men in black hoodies stealing a Volkswagen Golf sedan that was parked in a busy Chicago street.
Experts assume the thieves used an electronic device to capture and relay the frequencies of the vehicle’s key fob.
Six vehicles were stolen from Twin Auto Sales, a Detroit-area car dealership through a keyless theft device.

The thieves stole a black 2020 Dodge Durango SRT, a black 2017 Jeep Grand Cherokee SRT, a red 2014 Jeep Grand Cherokee SRT, a red 2020 Dodge Charger Scat Pack, a red 2018 Dodge Challenger R/T, and a black 2015 Dodge Challenger Hellcat.
According to the dealership owner, the six vehicles were worth about $50,000 each.

entities.text: control the Tesla Model S vehicle

text: Researchers analyzed Tesla's undocumented API and found unique exploits to control the Tesla Model S vehicle remotely through the API.

The researchers demonstrated that they could control the vehicle's motion and steering through the API, and that they were able to unlock the vehicle and flash the vehicle's headlights using the same method.
An Indian gang used sophisticated tools including a chip-reader and a hacking system, which included software available online, to steal more than 200 vehicles.
The thieves procured different keys online and transferred the vehicles' sensor coding to those keys, effectively duplicating the real key.
Masked car thieves stole a £17,000 Nissan from its owner's driveway in less than a minute by using a relay device to scan the key fob through the front door.
The burglars were caught on CCTV using an aerial relay to steal the vehicle from outside the property in the West Midlands, UK.
Intel’s security teams identified a potential security vulnerability in the Intel Advanced Driver Assistance Systems Innovation Engine (ADAS IE) firmware that may allow escalation of privilege.

entities.text: take control of the automated driving

text: With this vulnerability, a hacker could potentially take control of the automated driving elements of the vehicle.
Researchers found a vulnerability in OBDeleven OBD-II which allowed hackers to unlock its premium features free of charge.
The OBD-II is controlled via a bluetooth connected app which requires a paid subscription, allowing in-depth access to the ECU for advanced diagnostics and configurations.
However, the connection to the ECU was done via the app’s API, regardless of the payment status, and the vulnerability allowed users to use the app directly via the API without making a payment.
In addition to the financial damage to the company, the vulnerability opened an entry point for attackers to access the ECU and inject messages.
A researcher discovered vulnerabilities in Tesla Model X cars and their keyless entry fobs and was able to fully unlock, start, and steal a vehicle.

Tesla designed its Model X key fobs to receive over-the-air firmware updates via Bluetooth by wirelessly connecting to the computer inside a Model X, but without confirming that the new firmware code included unforgeable cryptographic signature from Tesla.
The researcher built a custom-made $300 Tesla Model X hacking tool which included a Model X body control module, a disassembled key fob, a Raspberry Pi minicomputer, and a battery.

The researcher used a personal computer with a Bluetooth radio to connect to a target Model X's keyfob, rewrite the firmware, query the secure enclave chip inside the fob that generated an unlock code for the vehicle, and then sent that code back to the personal computer via Bluetooth.
The whole process took 90 seconds.
Researchers from Consumer Watchdog claimed that they hacked a Tesla vehicle using a device that infiltrated the cellular network.

In a video, the researchers demonstrated that they could take over the infotainment screen in the Tesla to access the CAN-BUS and claimed that they could perform a wide-scale attack by amplifying the signal on the device.

Viewers however, claimed that the hack seen in the video showed a Wi-Fi server that could intercept the network requests sent to Tesla and thus caused the red hacked message to be displayed on the screen.
Researchers reverse engineered the Android head unit system of KIA Cee'd, exploited the vehicle's ability to install third-party applications, and instead installed an app containing malware.

entities.text: modify some of the IVI functionalities
switch the infotainment on and off

text: They exploited a previously discovered root privilege escalation vulnerability and created an exploit that could inject CAN frames to the M-bus and modify some of the IVI functionalities, such as manipulating the radio volume, switch the infotainment on and off, activate the reverse camera, and set a navigation address.
Inchcape, an Australian independent international automotive retailer, with operations in nearly 30 countries, was hit by the Windows Ransomexx ransomware.
In the attack, company data was stolen, including administration, customer fulfilment and client information, some of which was then leaked on the dark web.

Second-hand Tesla owners are jailbreaking the vehicles’ software in order to restore features like autopilot and supercharging that Tesla remotely disabled after the vehicle’s warranty and/or ownership changed.
One of the hackers claims he was able to restore the supercharging feature for more than 600 Teslas.
Officers launched early-morning raids on 21 locations in Essex and East London as part of an investigation into gang related thefts of luxury cars including Jaguars, Range Rovers, and BMWs.
At least twelve arrests were made in the raids.
The police suspect the gang is responsible for up to 90 thefts of vehicles, worth between £3-4 million, over less than two years.
In the raids, the police uncovered key cloning equipment, signal jamming equipment, and devices used to produce new keys for vehicles that were stolen.
Security researchers at the Sky-Go team found 19 vulnerabilities in a Mercedes-Benz E-Class car, allowing them to open its doors remotely and start the engine.
The researchers gained access to the car's backend servers by reverse-engineering the vehicle's embedded SIM card, which connects to the cellular network.
They communicated with the Mercedes backend servers and spoofed legitimate requests of Mercedes App users correlated to a different car.
For legal reasons, the research team only tested the vulnerabilities in China.
An artist manipulated Google Maps' navigation system by slowly pulling a wagon filled with 99 phones through a vacant Berlin street.
The hacker/artist tricked the maps app into “thinking” there was a traffic gridlock, essentially creating a virtual traffic jam.
Because of this manipulated “traffic jam”, the app redirected vehicles to alternative routes perceived by the app as more efficient.
If replicated, this could create real traffic jams in those rerouted areas and slow down traffic in a city.
A vehicle lessee, who had returned his car 4 years prior, was able to login to the myford.com mobile platform using credentials from 2016.
Logging into the portal, he was then able to lock and unlock the vehicle, start the engine, and remotely track its location and current usage.
The issue was discovered when he received an email update from Ford stating that the clock in his car was set incorrectly.
Tracker, a South African company operating a vehicle recovery service was hacked by ransomware, disrupting customer access to its services.
To stop the spread of the ransomware across the network, the company took its systems offline, thereby causing a service disruption.
Additionally, the company operates a telematic server to track and analyze its customer's vehicle usage and has over a million subscribers.
It has not yet been disclosed if customers’ sensitive data was compromised during the attack.
Toll Group, an Australian transportation company, was struck by a targeted ransomware attack leading the company to disable their systems as a precautionary measure.
The shutdown impacted several of its customer-facing applications and created a delay in the company's operations, forcing the company to return to manual processing.
The ransomware is believed to have infected as many as 1,000 servers, including Active Directory and corporate VPN, affecting the company's 40,000 employees.
Researchers from McAfee were able to fool an autonomous vehicle’s driver assist system by manipulation of the camera.
The researchers placed a small piece of tape horizontally across a 35 mile-per-hour speed limit sign.
The change caused the vehicle to read the limit as 85 miles per hour, and its cruise control system automatically accelerated.
The tests involved a 2016 Model S and Model X that used camera systems supplied by Mobileye Inc.
Two hackers connected a USB Ethernet adapter with a built-in backdoor to access Kenya’s NTSA network and databases.
Since the hackers possessed a compressor machine used for painting number plates, the hackers most likely used NTSA’s portal to illegally register stolen vehicles.

entities.text: bypass the access pin and prompt
remotely control various Ford vehicle functions

text: A custom open source mobile app enables users to bypass the access pin and prompt required by Fordpass to then remotely control various Ford vehicle functions.
In order to issue commands, the open source app simply requires configuring Fordpass credentials and VIN.
Then, the open source app sends HTTP requests directly to Fordpass’s API.
Users of the open source app can retrieve the vehicle status information, start and stop the engine, and issue lock/unlock commands to the vehicle.
Deploying the custom app on cloud platforms enables the users to create a shortcut on their mobile and even issue voice commands to the vehicle using SIRI.

RailWorks Corporation, one of North America’s leading railroad track and transit system providers, experienced a ransomware attack that led to the exposure of personally identifiable information of current and former employees, as well as that of independent contractors.
The ransomware harvested the information before encrypting the files.
The attackers might have gained access to names, addresses, driver license numbers, government-issued IDs, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and dates of hire or retirement.
Hackers launched a DDoS attack against German food delivery service Takeaway.com (Liefrando.de), demanding two bitcoins (about $11,000) to stop the flood of traffic.
Liefrando delivers food from more than 15,000 restaurants in Germany, where people under COVID-19 restrictions depend on the service.
The founder of the company posted about the attack via Twitter and included a note from the attackers indicating they planned to target other websites.
A researcher discovered a vulnerability in Tesla model 3 browser which allowed hackers to deny some of the services in the vehicle's driving interface.

entities.text: routing the vehicle’s browser traffic to a malicious website

text: By routing the vehicle’s browser traffic to a malicious website, attackers would be able to disable the speedometer, web browser, climate controls, turn signals, navigation, autopilot notifications, and blinker notifications along with other functions from the main screen.
The vulnerability was due to improper process separation in Tesla model 3.
Researchers performed a comprehensive security analysis of 77 wireless OBD-II dongles available on Amazon in the US in 2019.
The results identified 5 different types of vulnerabilities, 4 of which were newly discovered.
Each of the 77 dongles had at least two types of vulnerabilities indicating a widespread vulnerability exposure among wireless OBD-II dongles on the market today.
Nearly all dongles had no default connection layer authentication, allowing a potential attacker access to the CAN bus in the broadcast stage.

entities.text: didn’t filter out undefined CAN messages

text: Most dongles didn’t filter out undefined CAN messages, making them vulnerable to undefined malicious CAN injections.
Some of the dongles allowed multiple connections at once, allowing an attack against the vehicle even with the owner’s mobile device connected.
Additionally, the researchers managed to successfully install malicious over-the-air firmware upgrades to three dongles lacking FOTA authentication mechanisms.
Researchers discovered that the remote keyless system on Honda HR-V 2017 vehicles sends the same RF signal for each door-open request.

Once an attacker obtains the frequency of the key fob and captures the “open door” transmission sent from the fob, they can re-use the “open door” signal in a replay attack as the RF signal sent by the fob doesn't vary.
Other car models made by the OEM may have the same keyless system and therefore be prone to replay attacks.
A researcher reverse engineered the memory, the graphic interface, and the firmware of an OBD-II reader and turned the device into a custom attack tool.
The tool allowed attackers to upload payloads into the device, select them from a selection menu on the device's graphic interface, and run them on the vehicle.
The researcher also demonstrated the ability to draw images on the screen of the device.
Researchers observed APT41 exploiting vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler/ADC, Cisco routers, and Zoho ManageEngine Desktop Central as part of a widespread espionage campaign.
The campaign targeted companies from varying industries, including worldwide manufacturing and transportation companies.

Researchers demonstrated their ability to exploit a Bluetooth code execution vulnerability to compromise the infotainment unit of Lexus NX300 and send diagnosis messages to the internal CAN network and related ECUs.
In order to bypass the infotainment’s CAN message filtering capability, the researchers updated the firmware of one of the microcontrollers.

The researchers also designed the code executed to automatically connect to a Wi-Fi hotspot, enabling them to send diagnostic commands that could trigger a car with physical motions through the Wi-FI.
The vulnerable component in the infotainment was installed in Lexus (LC, LS, NX, RC, RC F), Toyota Camrys, and Toyota Siennas.
Thieves broke into a high-end BMW and stole two laptops from the vehicle's trunk.
It is assumed that the thief used a wireless signal jammer device to break into the vehicle, as no physical damage to the car was reported.

While assessing the security features of 13 new cars, Thatcham Research found that though progress is being made by carmakers, 7 out of the 13 new models they inspected were still coming to market with inherent vulnerabilities in their entry systems.
Four vehicles inspected did not pass the Thatcham relay theft tests.
These include: Mazda CX-30, MG HS Excite T-GDI, Subaru Forester e-Boxer XE Premium, and Vauxhall Corsa Ultimate Turbo 100.
Hyundai i10 Premium Mpi, MG HS Excite T-GDI, and Tesla Model 3 received a basic rating for passing the relay theft, yet were still missing certain traditional security features.
Tesla will apply additional security features on its next firmware upgrade and its rating will change accordingly.
Visser Precision, a parts contractor for Tesla was hit by a “cybersecurity incident,” which led to exposure of confidential documents belonging to the OEM.
Visser Precision’s incident was likely caused by the information stealing ransomware “DoppelPaymer”.
Researchers who create autonomous pilots for comma.ai demonstrated they were able to control the steering through Flexray network commands.
In order to reverse engineer the steering messages, the researchers created and open sourced a FlexRay decoder.

They discovered that the steering messages on Audi Q8’s flexray protocol closely matched CAN steering messages that they were familiar with, and applied their previous experience to manipulate the bytes in the messages on the FlexRay bus to control the Electric power assisted steering.
Compared to CAN, the FlexRay protocol is a lot stricter on timing which makes transmission of arbitrary messages through the network more challenging.
To make the demonstration more intriguing, the researchers programmed a joystick to send the steering commands.
Using a relay device, thieves unlocked and stole a Range Rover parking outside its owner's home in the West Midlands, UK.
Unauthenticated users were able to execute code on remote servers of fleet management and maintenance software, Fleetco.
The original exploit demonstrated how an attacker could create new accident records.
Israeli ride hailing app Bubble Dan misconfigured the server storing the receipts generated by the app, exposing receipts with PII and payment details of the app's users.

entities.text: changing the unique payment identifier parameter

text: By changing the unique payment identifier parameter in the link to the receipt, an unsophisticated attacker could easily scrape the receipt PDF files.
Each receipt contains the name, email, and the last four digits of the payment card used for the service.
In less than 3 minutes, a BMW M2 was stolen from its owners driveway in Poland using a relay device.

According to the owner, the car was located roughly 90-minutes after the theft just 40 km (25 miles) away from his home after being ditched by the thieves, perhaps because they thought the vehicle was being tracked.
The car was found with a newly replaced German license plate.

entities.text: crack the secret cryptographic key value

text: Millions of cars using chip-enabled mechanical keys implement the DST80 cryptographic algorithm in a way that allows an attacker to easily crack the secret cryptographic key value.
Some of the inspected fobs created their cryptographic key based on openly transmitted information, such as their serial number.
Other key fobs used 24 bits of randomness rather than the 80 bits that the DST80 offers, making their secret values easy to brute force.
Combining these cryptographic flaws with a little old-fashioned hot-wiring—or even a well-placed screwdriver—lets hackers clone those keys and drive away in seconds.
“Ghost rider” accounts are taking over the Russian car sharing apps, with many professionals selling accounts for less than 5 thousand rubles (about $66 USD).
The accounts utilized passport and credit card information bought from the dark web.
Since the service is cheap, people under the driving age limit set by the app often purchase these accounts to bypass the app's driving age verification.
One victim had to pay 14 thousand rubles for a Mercedes that was rented in his name.
A Moldovan man was jailed for ten months after using a relay amplifying device to steal multiple luxury keyless cars in the UK, including a £37,000 BMW.
In addition to the relay device, the police discovered the thief held a GPS jamming device, designed to block the GPS signals sent by the vehicle so it couldn’t be tracked once stolen.

A hacker modified his OBD dongle to expose the serial lines between its ELM327 OBD chip and its Bluetooth chip and used them to connect to an Arduino powering an information display on the vehicle's dashboard.

The device displayed information of some of the ECU units installed in the vehicle, including the battery voltage, RPM, MAP, Spark advance, intake temperature, engine coolant temperature, and information from the throttle position sensor.

entities.text: exposed the activity and private information

text: The My Renault app had an unsecured S3 bucket that exposed the activity and private information of the app's hundreds of thousand users in India.
The information included personal details of the customers such as: name, email, phone, address, login details and all of the recorded user interactions with the app and its services.
Researchers found a vulnerability in Volkswagen Polo’s infotainment software update process and were able to exploit it to hack the unit.
They also discovered that the infotainment unit used third-party software libraries that had known security flaws.
The researchers also analyzed Ford Focus and identified what is suspected to be a Wi-Fi password from Ford's manufacturing plant.
Using basic equipment, the hackers were able to intercept the messages being sent from the (Ford) tyres' TPMS to the car’s brain.
The researches also bought a second-hand infotainment unit and discovered the previous owner’s personal details.

entities.text: Project Worlds Official Car Rental System

text: A researcher discovered two vulnerabilities in "Project Worlds Official Car Rental System 1" (an open-sourced platform used to create car rental sites).
The first vulnerability allows unprivileged attackers to remotely read, delete, or modify the information in the app through SQL injection.

entities.text: upload and execute an arbitrary file

text: The second vulnerability allows a remote privileged user to upload and execute an arbitrary file on the app.
Aebi Schmidt announced that its systems were hit by a malware-based cyber attack.
The malware infected Windows systems and disrupted some of the company's operations, such as email management.
They had to temporarily switch off the affected systems.
A Polish gang of seven men stole millions of dollars worth of vehicles using relay amplifiers.
Because the thieves didn’t have a copy of the key fob, they weren't able to switch the vehicle off after they were stolen.
The thieves had to drive the vehicles non-stop to their destination directly and had to leave the engine on even when refueling.
A new keyfob was probably programmed at the destination.
The gang stole Audi brand vehicles and operated during nighttime.

entities.text: gain full control of the network

text: Researchers reverse-engineered a TCU of a vehicle and discovered that they were able to utilize the telematics connection to infiltrate the corporate network and gain full control of the network using admin credentials.

By pulling out the SIM card from the TCU and plugging it to a laptop, the researchers were able to utilize the SIM's access to the telematics private APN, which was connected to the telematics backend using a VPN.
Since the VPN had no significant segregation from the rest of the corporate network, the researchers were able to access the corporate network and servers outside the TCU backend.
CivicSmart, a vendor that sells parking meters capable of processing mobile payments, was hit last month with a form of ransomware known alternatively as Sodinokibi or REvil.
The hackers intended to publish as much as 159 gigabytes of data including credit card numbers of the company’s customers, employee records and contracts with cities and parking-garage vendors.
Messages posted to the hackers website suggest that CivicSmart paid an unspecified amount to take the files down from the hackers.
Sheffield City Council's automatic number-plate recognition (ANPR) system exposed 8.6 million records of road journeys made by thousands of people to the internet.
The ANPR camera system's internal management dashboard was left unsecured and could have been accessed by simply entering its IP address into a web browser.
Anyone who had access to the IP address could view and search the live system which logs where and when vehicles travel through Sheffield's road network.
A family-owned Massachusetts trucking company was a victim of a ransomware attack by the malware Maze.
The carrier’s system was locked down for more than a week and more than 781 megabytes of the company’s data was released on publicly accessible web pages.
The Texas Department of Transportation’s network was hacked in a “ransomware event".
Upon detecting the hack, staff at the transportation department immediately isolated the affected parts of the network.
The department’s website says some features are unavailable due to technical difficulties, but it is not clear what functions were affected by the attack.
2 years after hacking Indian car-rental platform, Zoomcar, the hackers publicly offered the information of 3.5 million app users for sale on the dark web.
The hackers waited two years before making the offer public to avoid being caught by officials tracking their IP addresses.
For $300, one can buy the usernames, passwords, emails, phone numbers, and IP addresses and potentially use the information to hack accounts on other platforms.
Car thieves smashed the window of a £46,000 Audi in Birmingham and started the car using a relay gadget bought online.
It took the thieves 40 seconds in total to start the car's engine and drive away.
A researcher used open-sourced hardware and software to build an OBD-II device to intercept CAN messages and send the information to the cloud.
The tool used a cellular modem to transmit a vehicle's GPS coordinates, RPM, speed, and temperature in real-time allowing the owner to monitor the vehicle remotely.
A vehicle was stolen in Bonnevoie, Luxemburg via a keyless theft gadget and was tracked using a smartphone app that allowed the owner to locate the car.
The vehicle was recovered in France a few days after the theft.
A tool created by researchers enables steering control for Tesla models that were built without the Autopilot feature.
The self-driving capabilities in these earlier Tesla models are limited by the gateway, and typically a message is sent indicating that steering over CAN is disabled.
The newly created tool patches the firmware and alters the message to allow steering over CAN and connection to a Comma.ai device.
In less than a week, two vehicles in the Milton Keynes region in the UK were stolen using relay devices.
Both thefts occurred during the nighttime.
While driving away, one of the cars stalled and the thieves, unable to restart it, fled, leaving the car abandoned on the road.
A vulnerability in ARMv7 implementation of GNU C Library leaves smart vehicles open to attack through a vulnerable web server exposed through the vehicle’s Wi-Fi network.
The vulnerability causes the program execution to continue with corrupted runtime state and allows exploitation after gaining access to the vehicle’s Wi-Fi network.
Exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to undefined behavior such as writing to out-of-bounds memory and potentially remote code execution on the vehicle.
A researcher created a tool that faked the RPM displayed in the dashboard of his old Mercedes to make the gear transmission seem quicker than it was.
The tool crafted CAN BUS messages according to the target gear and changed the value displayed RPM according to the target gear.
A researcher discovered a vulnerability in the ‘Car Rental System’ plugin for WordPress.
Persistent XSS can occur in most of the fields in the booking form.
XSS can lead to an administrator’s session hijacking, and if used with a social engineering attack, it can also lead to disclosure of sensitive data, CSRF attacks, and other critical attacks.
Visitors to several infected sites, including a store selling auto parts, were victims of a phishing campaign informing them that their security certificate has expired.
The campaign overlayed the website's content with a legitimate-looking banner prompting the users to install an updated certificate claiming that their certificate has expired.
By clicking install, users downloaded malware directly to their computer.
Thames Valley, UK Police released videos documenting four different cases of keyless theft that occurred in South Oxfordshire and the Vale of White Horse region.
Three BMWs were stolen, including a BMW M4.
It is believed the offenders used scanning devices to steal the vehicle from its driveway.
London's Metropolitan Police reported that a Ford S Max was stolen with a keyless hacking device.
The West Midlands police reported that they recovered a Ford Fiesta stolen using a keyless theft device.
A researcher was able to hack into Uber using a vulnerability in Portainer, a Docker container management system.
The vulnerability in Portainer allows remote attackers to bypass access restrictions to the Docker API or conduct SSRF attacks.
The researcher exploited the SSRF vulnerability to make arbitrary requests to the local Docker API and proved that he was able to run remote commands on the host.
Car thieves have made off with five expensive motors - using a device that mimics a keyless fob.
The cars were stolen from multiple driveways in the UK.
A group of hackers recently hacked one of Mercedes-Benz's official Instagram accounts.
The hackers posted BMW promotions through the account and also changed the name, profile picture, and bio, requesting Bitcoin donations for supposed Coronavirus pandemic victims.
The hackers also posted a picture of a swastika.
B-H Transfer, a US-based trucking company, was targeted by ransomware in February, just as COVID-19 spread across the US.
The attackers penetrated the company's backup files, deleted, and encrypted them.
It took the company almost two weeks to restore its systems to the original state.

Security experts have discovered old Tesla car parts for sale on eBay that still contained user data belonging to the previous owner, in a sign that the firm’s retrofitting service is failing customers on privacy.
Some of the resold infotainment contents were phone books, hundreds of call log entries, calendar entries, home, and work locations.
The units were loaded with Gmail accounts, YouTube, and Netflix session cookies.
The researcher also discovered readable Wi-Fi and Spotify passwords.
After recovering from a cyber attack in the beginning of 2020, Toll Group systems were hit by a new ransomware attack.
After detecting unusual activity on the company’s servers, the company shut down some IT systems as a precaution.
In the attack, some online customer applications were taken offline, and Toll's staff had to rely on personal computers and devices, as they were unable to work from company PCs.
International rail vehicle construction company, Stadler, disclosed that it was the victim of a cyberattack in which attackers may have stolen company and employee data.
The hackers attempted to blackmail the company, demanding large sums of money, and put pressure on Stadler by threatening to publish the private data.
A former police officer was involved in the theft of 10 vehicles across Peterborough, UK between June and October 2019.
The thief used a £15,000 relay device that required working with a partner to capture the vehicles.
The former officer left the stolen vehicles in communal car parks to allow time for any GPS system to track them down.
Six vehicles were recovered, but untraced vehicles were dismantled and exported in parts to Eastern Europe and Africa.
A hacker published the full content of a GitLab server containing detailed information on a Mercedes OLU component, which simplifies access and management of live vehicle data.
The server contained all of the 580 repositories related to the OLU, including images, code, detailed documentation, and development environments.
The researcher was able to access the server by registering with a non-existent Daimler corporate email and decided to share the information on multiple file sharing sites.
Another researcher claims he discovered passwords and API tokens for Daimler's internal systems in the repository.
If attained by the wrong hands, these passwords and access tokens could be used to plan and mount future intrusions against Daimler's cloud and internal network.
Anonymous hackers have taken the data of over 129 million Russian car owners and offered to expose it on the darknet in exchange for cryptocurrency.
The leaked information includes the full names, addresses, passport numbers, and other data belonging to millions of Russian car drivers.

entities.text: General Administration for Traffic Safety of the Ministry

text: The stolen data is claimed to be leaked from the registry of Russia’s patrol jurisdiction, the General Administration for Traffic Safety of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Russia.
The full version of the database costs 0.3 BTC, which amounts to about $2,900 .
The hackers also offered “exclusive” data for sale at 1.5 BTC ($14,400).

entities.text: Traffic Light and Stop Sign Control

text: Tesla’s " Traffic Light and Stop Sign Control " feature confuses Burger King signs for stop signs, causing the vehicle to slow down when capturing the sign from a distance.
While this event was not an intentional cyber manipulation, black hat actors might try to re-use this technique and create malicious signs that will disrupt vehicles on the road.
A hacking group offered a database of BMW car owners for sale on the dark web.
The group claimed that the database contained 384,319 records from a “call center” that managed customers of different car suppliers.

A research company that obtained the database found that it contained almost 500,000 customer records from 2016 to 2018, including details of U.K owners of Mercedes, Seat, Honda, Hyundai, and other vehicle brands.
Car thieves targeted vehicles in the Bishopbriggs and Bearsden areas of Scotland using relay devices.
According to the police, six Ford vehicles of varying types, from Mondeos to Transit vans, were stolen from driveways and outside homes.
In the wider Glasgow area, 13 cars were stolen in a span of only two days.
In an attempt to mimic a Heads Up Display (HUD) on a C6 Corvette, a hacker built a custom HUD that showed the vehicle’s speed and RPM on a transparent display mounted on a dashboard.

The hacker collected the RPM and the speed of the vehicle with a Bluetooth OBD-II reader and then transferred the details to a development board that recorded the vehicle data to a SD card and another MCU that ran the actual LED displayed in the HUD.
Researchers identified two vulnerabilities in MAVLink, a protocol designed for communication with unmanned vehicles.

The first vulnerability is the protocol's lack of encryption, which allows a remote attacker who has access to the communication medium access to sensitive information by intercepting the unencrypted messages.

The second vulnerability is that the protocol lacks an authentication system and is therefore vulnerable to a variety of attacks, including identity spoofing, unauthorized access, MITM attacks, and more.
A hacker demonstrated how Nissan Leaf owners could pair newly installed batteries while avoiding the 'invalid battery' trouble code that reduces the vehicle's performance.
In order to clear the trouble code, the vehicle control module ECU had to acknowledge the new battery ID.
The hacker demonstrated two methods to do it: The first method is to replace the LBC (Lithium Battery Control) ECU into the new battery.
The second method is initiating a MITM attack through the vehicle's CAN-bus.

By spoofing the ID of the previous battery on the messages sent by the newly installed one, the ID on the CAN-Bus will match the one stored in the VCM ECU and will allow the vehicle to operate as if the new battery was programmed by the OEM.
A £120,000 Range Rover Autobiography was stolen from a supermarket parking lot in Walthamstow, London.
The theft took a mere 80 seconds when thieves took advantage of weaknesses in the keyless entry system.
The vehicle was recovered by the Metropolitan Police within 12 hours, due to a tracking device in the vehicle.
Croydon, London’s local police reported an increased number of car theft cases using relay devices.
BMW vehicles, Ford Fiestas and Focus were all victims of the recent keyless theft incidents.
The police claimed that the vehicles were stolen to facilitate further crime, including catalytic converter theft, vehicle crime, metal thefts, and burglaries.
A hacker installed a custom infotainment system in his Toyota that enabled control over the ignition module and the vehicle's AC.
The infotainment also allowed the changing of the honk sound and allowed honking through the infotainment instead of the steering wheel.
The vehicle had to be immobilized with its key fob for the device to work.

To get accurate notifications on his vehicle charging status, a hacker reversed engineered BMW's connected drive and created an open-sourced app that actively retrieves real-time charging information from his vehicle using BMW's API.
To use the app, users must configure their credentials to authenticate with BMW's API.
With some additional development, the app could also allow control of BMW's other connected API features - activation of headlights, horns, and unlock/lock commands through the open sourced app.
Hackers attacked the website of the UzAuto automaker (formerly known as GM Uzbekistan).

The attack caused a temporary malfunction of the site, but due to the efforts of the company's IT experts, not a single file or page on the site were damaged, and the site resumed operations after a short period of time.
Researchers found an exploitable code execution vulnerability in the web-based management of WAGO's programmable automation controllers, used in the automotive industry.

entities.text: specially crafted series of HTTP requests

text: The vulnerability allows a specially crafted series of HTTP requests to cause local code execution resulting in remote code execution.
A researcher gained access to Tesla's cloud IT service management tool and was able to retrieve sensitive information from the system.
He found the credentials to the system in a public Github repository.

Though logging into the system from its standard user interface requires multi-factor authentication, the researcher proved he was able to bypass it by crafting requests directly to the IT service API.
A motivated attacker could use this access to view help desk tickets that were issued, and map Tesla’s internal servers, IP addresses, and issues reported to Tesla’s system administors.
Researchers found security issues in a vehicle fine enforcement clamp that communicates via cellular network.
They were able to use the SIM card to discover the barnacle's API and gain access to the entire environment by refreshing a request 10 times.

entities.text: control all of the parking clamps

text: Malicious hackers could have exploited this access to control all of the parking clamps and leak user data.

The researchers also discovered they were able to unlock the barnacles for free, as the payment gateway didn't validate the credit card effectively, and also discovered that one of the S3 buckets was wide open and indexed by Google.
Honda's networks in Europe and Japan were affected by issues reportedly related to a Snake Ransomware cyber-attack.
Unlike the typical ransomware, Snake is designed to attack industrial control systems and targets entire networks rather than individual workstations.
Honda stopped production in some of its plants for a few days due to the ransomware.
A Canadian company hacked Tesla’s software, and it is now offering some of its Tesla software performance upgrades at a discount.
The company offers an easily pluggable connector that cracks Tesla's 'acceleration boost' which unlocks roughly 50 hp in the Model 3 powertrain and shortens the acceleration.
The company also added an additional “drift mode” capability to those who purchase the “acceleration boost” package.

The company also offers to upgrade Model 3 Dual Motor vehicles to a Model 3 Performance, however, this service is more invasive, requires professional hardware installation, and will disable the capability to receive software updates from Tesla.
A researcher modified his motorcycle dashboard and added a custom shift notification by sending CAN-BUS messages.
The tool reacts to the RPM and causes the dashboard to flash yellow when the time comes to shift the gears.
The North Texas police tracked a group of car thieves that specifically targeted new-generation Nissan cars, using relay attacks to unlock the doors and cloned key fobs to start the engine.
After the vehicles were stolen, the thieves changed the vehicle identification numbers and sold the stolen vehicles to unsuspecting individuals at low prices.
The group managed to steal about 62 Nissan cars, worth more than $1.2 million.
A hacker reprogrammed the cruise control button on his steering wheel to control a newly installed Android head unit through the vehicle's CAN-bus.
Since the button was connected directly to an ECU, the hacker had to re-route the wires to communicate through the CAN bus.

The Android head unit received the CAN commands sent from the steering wheel due to a keyboard emulator that converted the CAN Command to emulated keyboard signals and transferred the controls to the head unit.
Researchers identified two vulnerabilities in robotic fleet vehicles made by Model Industrial Robots.
One of the wireless interfaces in MiR200 and MiR100 robots, come with a pre-configured Wi-Fi mode that has well known credentials.
Moreover, the vehicle’s control dashboard is accessible through a hardcoded IP address with widely spread credentials.

entities.text: take control of the robot remotely

text: This flaw allows attackers to take control of the robot remotely and make use of the default user interfaces MiR has created, lowering the complexity of attacks and making them available to entry-level attackers.
More elaborated attacks can also be established by clearing authentication and sending network requests directly.
A researcher created a mobile phone sized attack device that jams the Collision Avoidance System (CAS) in autonomous vehicles from a relatively short distance.
He was able to cause an accident by making the forward collision warning (FCW) and autonomous emergency braking (AEB) less sensitive and slow to respond.

He demonstrated the attack on a Tesla Model 3 and Lynk&Co 01 and provided tools to assist other researchers to find the vehicle's collision avoidance system radar parameter, facilitating future attacks on autonomous vehicles.
A Polish criminal network stole at least 34 cars worth $1.6 million using keyless technologies.
The thieves used "technical equipment" to crack the vehicle's “KEYLESS GO” systems.
The police were able to identify that at least 13 of the vehicles were dismantled into parts by the thieves, who manually removed identification numbers from the parts.
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) stated they were victims of a ransomware attack on their email server.
The ransomware operators breached NHAI servers and released sensitive data files.
The ransomware operators claim to have uploaded 100% of the total data leak.

The data leak included sensitive corporate operational documents such as the company's staff list, a passport copy of the former chairman of NHAI, details of dependent family members of NHAI employees, NHAI internal audit reports, and more.
The two high-value Range Rovers and a top-of-the-range Mercedes-Benz were stolen by thieves.

The thieves had disabled the OEM vehicle tracking services but had missed the dedicated aftermarket telematics tracking devices, which enabled the vehicles to be located in containers at Ilford, Essex, ready for shipping abroad.
ADIF, a Spanish state-owned railway infrastructure management system, was hit by REVil ransomware operators.
The hackers claimed to have stolen 800GB of data, including correspondence and contracts.
As proof of the attack, the ransomware operators posted a sample of files exfiltrated from the company, and threatened to release confidential data online if a ransom was not paid.
Toyota revealed that researchers found a buffer overflow vulnerability in the Global TechStream (GTS) diagnostic cable.
The vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (DoS) condition.

A hacker made the Mercedes' MBUX infotainment system work on an old Mercedes W203 through an Arduino linked to the CAN bus which decoded CAN frames and sent them to the Android tablet over a USB connection.
He was able to display live information on the vehicle’s fuel usage, climate control, and window state.
An officer reported that a Mercedes GLS350 was stolen via keyless theft from outside the owner's house in Newham, UK.
The car was found with a false license plate within 20 minutes of the theft.
An issue was discovered on Realtek RTL8195AM, RTL8711AM, RTL8711AF, and RTL8710AF devices.
A stack-based buffer overflow exists in the client code that takes care of WPA2's 4-way-handshake via a malformed EAPOL-Key packet with a long keydata buffer.
These devices are highly popular standalone, low-power-consumption WiFi hardware modules, used for embedded devices in several industries such as the agriculture, healthcare, and automotive sectors.

BCycle, a corporation that operates bicycle sharing service, found malware on its website that allowed a hacker to find personal information of users who signed up for a membership pass through the company's website.
The breached information may have included users' names, credit card numbers, and addresses.
The company claimed to cover the cost of one year of identity theft protection for affected customers.
The cybercriminals behind the malicious encryptor NetWalker hacked Trinity Metros, a Texas based transit agency and threatened to release all their data unless the company gave them money.
The criminal group posted screenshots of the victim’s encrypted files on their online blog on the dark-web.
Examples of the folder names, which offer a hint of the content inside, include "Accounting and HR Shared," "Daily Operations Documents," "Planning Documents," and "Security."
Egypt-based ride hailing app, SWVL, was hacked in a cyberattack that exposed the personal information of passengers, including emails, names, and phone numbers.
If abused, the hackers could sell the information on the dark web or use it to gain access to other accounts that belong to the victims using the password they got from SWVL.

entities.text: none of the dashcam recording outputs was signed

text: A researcher reversed engineered the content of Tesla's dashcam hard drive and found that none of the dashcam recording outputs was signed.
The researcher was able to edit the metadata related to the recordings including the date of the recording and its location and replace the MP4 video recordings.
As dashcam recordings are used in insurance claims as evidence for acts of theft, vandalism, or accidents, this vulnerability can cost a lot to insurers.
People can use this hack to replace the video and metadata of a dashcam recording with a similar vehicle that had a crash to get entitled for free repair if they have third party insurance.
A tech firm from Bulgaria is selling devices for car thieves which are strikingly similar to old Nintendo Game Boys consoles.
The company’s SOS Key Tool is marketed as ‘the most advanced locksmith tool’ available.
It is currently sold for £20,000, and unlike other popular devices, it doesn't require a relay from a nearby key fob to unlock vehicles.
The gadget records the car’s data and acts as a responder which the vehicle recognizes as an authorized remote.
The car will unlock and start as if the thief had a valid key fob.
A tutorial video on YouTube shows how it can be used to unlock modern Kia, Hyundai, and Mitsubishi models within a minute.
Researchers discovered a LDAP injection vulnerability in Traccar GPS Tracking System.
The issue occurs when user input is used in the LDAP search filter.
By providing specially crafted input, an attacker can modify the logic of the LDAP query and get admin privileges.
Toronto’s police released a video from a surveillance camera where thieves used a signal booster to steal a Lexus vehicle from the owner's driveway.

In the video, one of the thieves stood near the front door of the house and pulled out a device to capture the signal being emitted from the keyless fob, which was located near the inside entrance of the house.
The boosted signal unlocked the car and also started the vehicle’s engine, allowing the thieves to flee with the vehicle.
A researcher found a vulnerability in Tesla Model 3's NFC tag that allowed him to perform a relay attack.
By leveraging the signal of a legitimate NFC tag associated with the vehicle, the researcher was able to open the vehicle's door.
Due to the limitation of the NFC protocol, this attack required a proximity of 10cm to Tesla's NFC tag.
While reverse engineering Tesla's power improvements, a researcher discovered that the battery management system (BMS) defined the drive unit's power limit.
The researcher used CAN messages, UDS messages, firmware files, and decrypted diagnostic messages to reverse engineer the upgrade process.

He discovered which hardware changes were required in the BMS to execute the power improvement upgrade and performed them on a P85D. Later, he modified the firmware of the BMS and the relevant files on the security gateway to accept the modified battery pack.
He bricked the car during the firmware update process and had to troubleshoot it.
The ransomware operators behind Conti ransomware claimed that they breached the Volkswagen Group.
The ransomware operators appeared to have targeted one of the Volkswagen Group franchises based in Salzkotten, Germany.
As of August 2020, the data leak contained a combined total of 857 number of workshop services related to invoices and automotive part sales related invoices.
A hacker discovered a vulnerability in the Bluetooth stack of Mercedes-Benz C Class AMG Premium Plus c220 BlueTec.
Bluetooth connections with devices that contain format strings in the device name created an issue in the Bluetooth stack and caused the COMAND infotainment to behave unpredictably.
The hacker demonstrated that connecting a device with the strings "%x" or "%c" in the device name impacted the user interface of the infotainment.
A hacker exploited a vulnerability discovered in Tesla's server-side mechanism to access Tesla's network and view a repository of server images.

One of the servers accessed, named ‘Mothership', was the Command-and-Control server used to communicate with Tesla's customer fleet; Any kind of remote commands or diagnostic information from the car to Tesla goes through this server.
By reverse-engineering his car’s VPN connection to contact Mothership, the hacker landed on a developer network connection.
He found a critical bug in Mothership itself that enabled him to authenticate as any Tesla vehicle in the world.
The vulnerability allowed him to control and get information about any car in the fleet and send commands to those cars.

The police forces in Grimsby, UK, warned the owners of high-value cars to be extra vigilant after a rise in thefts throughout August 2020, as many keyless entry Land Rovers and Range Rovers were targeted by thieves.
Hackers are selling a database with information of a million Moscow region drivers for $1,500.
The information includes the full name of car owners, their phone numbers, the vehicle’s VIN, the vehicle's registration date, brand, model, and production year.
The information in the database is not up-to-date and only includes information from 2019 and earlier.
A researcher discovered that Power Line Communications ( PLC ) signals could be easily read using active antennas placed between 6-8 feet away from the trailer.
The cybersecurity impact of this vulnerability is heavily dependent on which information is sent by ECUs on the trailer PLC bus.
Typical trailer traffic includes only ABS fault messages and will thus have minimal loss of confidentiality.

However, the vulnerability can have a severe impact in cases where manufacturers leverage PLC for sensitive information such as air weight axles or key exchange in setting up high-speed wireless links in future tractor-trailer interfaces.
Operators of Netwalker ransomware claimed that they hacked and now possess the data of Forsee Power, a company that provides lithium-ion battery systems for mobility applications.
The operators shared a few screenshots as proof of access.

The screenshot displayed folders such as “Accounts Receivable”, “Finance”, “Collection Letters”, “Expenses”, “Employees”, and much more, implying the names of the departments that were affected by the breach.
Researchers discovered an information disclosure and remote code execution vulnerability in a web server in some versions of the BlackBerry QNX software development platform.
Blackberry's QNX is widely used in infotainment systems and digital instrument clusters, and the QNX SDP is aimed at supporting the development of connected car applications.
The vulnerability could potentially allow an attacker to read arbitrary files from Blackberry's QNX SDP and run arbitrary executables with the web server's privileges.
Hackers offered to sell VPN access to a major automotive manufacturer in South Korea.

The hackers were affiliated with the profitable hacking group FXMSP and presumably gained network access by exploiting a Pulse VPN vulnerability (CVE-2019-11510) and sustained access after the patch was applied.
A researcher who contacted one of the hackers identified Hyundai as the victim of the attack and received a screenshot with Hyundai’s host names as a proof of access to their network.
A Chinese Tesla car owner encountered a bug in the Tesla app, causing his vehicle to disappear from the app.
Instead, 5 other cars from Europe appeared in the app.
He was able to view all of the details on the car and remotely control them as if he owned them.
A group of researchers worked with more than 10 auto manufacturers and suppliers to assess the hardware and software of more than 40 ECUs in development.
Within those, they found over 300 vulnerabilities.
The researchers concluded that only 20% of the vulnerabilities found were related to hardware issues.

They assigned each vulnerability with a risk score according to ISO/SAE DIS 21434 and found that all vulnerabilities assigned with a high-risk score were a result of a fault in the software or OS of the ECU, and not related to hardware bugs.
The results highlight that the more complex an ECU is, the more vulnerabilities exist in it and the percentage of the high risk vulnerabilities rises.
Man and woman believe that an organized gang used key cloning equipment to steal their Nissan Qashqai SUV which was parked overnight at a hotel in a crime-ridden UK neighborhood.
Thousands of Utah drivers unintentionally purchased cars with hacked odometers.
Crooks tampered with analog as well as digital odometers, costing car buyers thousands of dollars and putting their safety at a high risk.

entities.text: National Highway Traffic and Safety Administration

text: The National Highway Traffic and Safety Administration estimates that 450,000 vehicles are sold each year with false odometer readings, costing American car buyers more than $1 billion annually.
A hacker modified his Casio F91W to use it as an NFC based vehicle key fob.

He used an open-sourced Java Card applet that emulates Tesla Model 3's key fob and relied on prior research that demonstrated how to add NFC capabilities into a Casio F91W. The modification was completely hidden, and the hacker claimed that the NFC communication with the vehicle was stable.
A large number of people who had their car stolen this year in Washington D.C. were using the carsharing app Getaround to rent out their personal vehicles and make extra money.
Since the start of 2020, more than 200 auto thefts have been reported to authorities in D.C. and more than 75 of the victims were Getaround users
In an attempt to prevent Nissan Leaf's battery degradation, a hacker developed a CAN-bridge to hack the CAN-messages between battery management and vehicle to avoid degradation.
Through hacking into the CAN-messages sent to the battery management system, the hacker was able to lower the charging speed and prevent the battery from heating, a primary cause of degradation.
The hacker offered the CAN-bridge and its software for sale at 450 Euro.
Researchers discovered a vulnerability in Android Auto settings which allowed permission bypass due to an unsafe Android reference token.
The privileges could allow a local information disclosure vulnerability, resulting in command execution privileges.
The vulnerability could locally trigger without user interaction.
Vehicle thieves in Kenya used jammers to steal vehicles.
As drivers parked and presumably locked their vehicles with key fobs, thieves jammed the signal, and though the car's alarm made its usual sound, the car did not lock.
The police claimed that the thieves also often disabled the car’s GPS trackers with jammers that were purchased online.

Nissan North America's source code of mobile apps and internal tools was leaked online, January 4th, as result of a misconfiguration of one of the company’s Git servers, leaving it exposed on the internet with default credentials: admin/admin.
Among the leaked data were the Nissan internal core mobile library, the vehicle logistics portal and some parts of the Nissan ASIST diagnostics tool.

Western Massachusetts police reported an increase in organized crime car thefts, where hackers have driven around neighborhoods and used devices to capture vehicle key fob signals, later returning with a copy of the unique frequency to unlock the cars and steal them.

The police also warned owners of push-to-start vehicles (where radio transmission of the key fob also acts as the engine switch) of the potential of having their cars quietly and easily stolen as well.
A security researcher hacked the lcn2kai Bosch infotainment unit in a Nissan Xterra vehicle.
The hacker found a vulnerability in the infotainment system where by plugging in a USB device, he was able to gain root shell access to the system.
The hacker added that Bosch's infotainment’s vulnerability may affect other Nissan models produced after 2015, including Rogue, Sentra, Altima, Frontier, as well as other Nissan commercial vehicles.
Night surveillance video captured thieves from South St.Louis, Missouri hacking into a Chevrolet SUV in what appeared to be a keyless entry relay attack.
At 3am, the hackers unlocked the victim’s vehicle and stole possessions from inside.
The theft was not an isolated incident; it was reported that several cars in the same area were hacked via a keyfob reader.
A vulnerability was found in a Qualcomm Snapdragon chip, a chip in use by OEMs to power in-vehicle infotainment and navigation as well as a 4G LTE modem for connectivity.
The vulnerability, in which a race condition occurs while calling user space input-output-control from two different threads, can cause issues in video related to the infotainment system.
The Snapdragon chip is used in many industries, including the automotive industry.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has asked Tesla to recall some 158,000 Model S and Model X vehicles that could suffer from failing display consoles.
The failures of the media control units in these vehicles could sever the owner’s access to their vehicle’s backup camera, climate controls, and Tesla’s Autopilot driver assistance system.
The problem at the heart of the defect that NHTSA wanted Tesla to fix involves worn-out flash memory chips used in the displays of 2012-2018 Model S sedans and 2016-2018 Model X SUVs.

Tesla confirmed to NHTSA that all units with this chip will inevitably fail, according to the agency, and also provided a statistical model showing projected weekly repairs lasting from 2020 to 2028, with the most failures happening in 2022.
Two vulnerabilities were found on a Vehicle Parking Management System.

The vulnerabilities were around SQL injection, which makes the system vulnerable to time-based SQL injection on multiple endpoints, and a stored cross site scripting ( XSS) in the sourcecodester Vehicle Parking Management System.
Halton Regional Police warned residents in Burlington, Oakville and Milton to take steps to avoid having their car stolen.
Thefts of vehicles, especially higher-end vehicles, were on the rise, with police reporting seven being stolen right from residential driveways during one overnight period.
According to the police, as vehicles relied more on keyless entry and remote starters, blackmarket technology to counter that had made stealing cars quicker and easier.
According to Staffordshire police, a number of targeted keyless car thefts were recorded, such as Fiat 500s and Ford Transit vans.
The police stated that 10 vans were stolen between July and September across the UK.
In late October 2021, Mercedes-Benz private data, including the company’s critical infrastructure platform and Beijing Benz Automotive API system, were leaked to the dark web.
The leaked data was composed in Chinese and English.

The second part of the leak contained code written in java that appeared to be still in development, including job sequence codes, email sending tasks, hardcoded serial version UID values, and basic functionality comments.

Incidents involving keyless starting fob systems have been rising in Canada as thieves use electronic devices to enter vehicles, start their engines and leave within minutes, leading to Ontario Provincial Police to issue a warning to vehicle owners.

According to the Canadian Automobile Association (CAA), the vehicle and fob communicate using low-power radio signals that are only effective within approximately 36 inches of the car door or ignition start/stop button and some thieves have developed special equipment to amplify the communication signals.
This tricks the car into thinking the fob is next to the car door or trunk, allowing the vehicle to be unlocked and started.
Six vehicles were stolen using relay and reprogramming technology, leading to a Brantford police investigation.
The stolen vehicles were two Lexus RX5s, three Toyota 4Runners, and a Toyota Highlander.
According to the police, the stolen vehicles were all new high-end models with keyless entry and push start technology.

In addition, they explained that suspects use technology to find a key fob signal inside homes and use that technology to amplify and transfer the key fob signal to unlock, start and steal the vehicles.

Furthermore, the police added that the suspects could also force entry inside a vehicle and use an electronic device to access diagnostics and they can reprogram a blank key fob to start the vehicle they plan to steal.
Three men were charged early October 2021 with using a Nintendo Game Boy to break into cars.
According to West Yorkshire Police, the offenders used a handheld gizmo that looked like a Nintendo Game Boy to fool the car’s keyless entry and ignition that a legitimate keyless fob was being used.

In addition, police say that from May through July of 2021, more than 30 Mitsubishi Outlanders were stolen, and that led to an investigation that ended up linking the three men to a conspiracy involving five separate vehicle thefts valued in excess of £180,000 ( over $330,000).
A team of Dutch forensic researchers reverse engineered a Tesla’s vehicles data storage system.
They discovered far more detailed data than expected, including speed, accelerator pedal position, steering wheel angle, and brake usage.
The team assessed the data instead of requesting it from Tesla following a crash that occurred while Autopilot was active.
The news of the hack could have implications for US investigators who are probing a dozen incidents of crashes involving Tesla vehicles and emergency vehicles while Autopilot was in use.
A vulnerability was found in the Bluetooth pairing dialog within the Android Automotive Operating System ( AAOS), allowing a hacker to enable Bluetooth without user consent.
The vulnerability can potentially lead to local escalation of privilege where user execution privileges are usually needed.
Italian State police arrested a 54-year-old suspect for aggravated theft after preventing vehicles from locking after the drivers exited their cars.
Immediately after drivers exited their vehicles, a signal jammer was used to prevent the car’s locking mechanism from engaging.
As the owners walked away the thief had ample time to enter the vehicle and manipulate the ignition system.
Hackers were believed to have used relay devices to hack and steal BMWs and Mercedes vehicles during a spate of keyless car thefts across the UK’s Hampshire district.
Local police stated that the hackers allegedly started the cars remotely via a relay device, which connected with the vehicle’s fob.
Among the stolen cars were a BMW 320d SE, a BMW 520d M Sport, a Mercedes GLC 250, a Mercedes GLE 250 AMG, a Mercedes AMG E63, and a Mercedes GLC 250.
Hackers armed with a relay device struck in a Birmingham suburb by simply waving a bag near a house to unlock and start the vehicle outside.
The October 13th CCTV footage showed a man holding a messenger-style bag up near the front of the home and front door until the white Kia Sportage opened and started.
In less than 60 seconds, a relay device in the bag triggered and repeated the car’s fob signal, allowing thieves to gain access and drive off.
Car thieves in a Birmingham road hacked and stole a Mercedes C Class Coupe using a relay attack station, despite not having the keys.

Attacks are carried out using two devices: the first device monitors the signals from the remote control key assigned to the car, and a second sends identical signals to the car.
Thames Valley Police urged citizens to keep their keyless fobs as far away as possible from their parked cars following a string of thefts across Berkshire where keyless cars have been stolen.
One incident involved a keyless Range Rover Velar which was stolen without the key fob on site.

The second vehicle was a keyless fob entry Land Rover which was tracked by the Land Rover tracking department who alerted the owner that it was driven without a fob inside the car, and believed it may have been stolen using a relay device.
An East London gang used high-tech gadgets to steal 25 luxury cars which were then sold with cloned plates or dismantled for parts.
The group of six men were all accused of being involved in the thefts, targeting expensive cars including an Audi S4, Land Rover Discovery, and a BMW X6.
Some of the thieves used blank fobs to connect to the car's central computer and reprogram it as a new key.
Hackers recently compromised and stole a BMW 420i in Neutraubling, Germany.

It is believed that the black-hat hackers entered using a short-range radio system, prompting police to advise drivers with keyless systems in their vehicles to park in locked indoor garages, not on the street.
Four vulnerabilities were found on Qualcomm Snapdragon chips.
