The vulnerabilities varied around integer overflow and heap overflow, as well as improper validations, some of which of P2P device address.
Twenty nine vulnerabilities were found on Qualcomm Snapdragon chips.
The vulnerabilities were on different chips, such as the Snapdragon Auto, Snapdragon Consumer IoT, and Snapdragon Industrial IoT.
Some of the vulnerabilities varied around memory corruptions, buffer over reads, buffer overflows, integer overflow, and sensitive information disclosures.
A vulnerability was found on a Vehicle Parking Management System.
The vulnerability is around the persistent cross site scripting ( XSS), which allows attackers to execute arbitrary web scripts or HTML via a crafted payload in the Category field.
Oakland county police arrested four people connected to the theft of four Dodge vehicles from a Highland Township dealership worth over $329,000.
The four cars - a 2021 Dodge Durango Hellcat SRT, a 2021 Dodge Durango GT, a 2021 Dodge Ram TRX, and a 2017 Dodge Charger Hellcat SRT - were all stolen from Szott Dodge in Highland Township.
Inside one of the located SUVs, the police found a computer device to reprogram key fobs.

According to the police, in a 6 month period, the group scoped out and targeted cars to steal, obtained key code information for these vehicles from unlawful websites, and created keys that allowed them to breach and steal the vehicles.

In addition, the Attorney General’s office added that once inside of the vehicle, the thieves allegedly reprogrammed the vehicle’s computer system to gain control of the vehicle, disable alarms, and start the engine.
In a matter of minutes, the theft crew was able to steal a vehicle without drawing any attention.
In addition, the theft crew reprogramed the vehicle to stop recognizing the true owners’ electronic keys.
Forescout Research Labs, with support from Medigate Labs, discovered a set of 13 new vulnerabilities affecting the Nucleus TCP/IP stack, collectively called NUCLEUS:13.
13 new vulnerabilities were identified that allow for remote code execution, denial of service, and information leaks from the Nucleus TCP/IP stack.
Discovered by Forescout Research Labs and Medigate Labs, Nucleus is used in safety-critical industries such as medical devices, automotive, and industrial systems.
Siemens released patches for all reported vulnerabilities.

On January 1st, 2022, Acura and Honda navigation system automatically changed to January 1st, 2002, with the time resetting to 12:00, 2:00, 4:00, or other times based on the model or possibly the region in which the car was located.
This happened after Honda and Acura cars were hit with the Y2K22 bug that reset the navigation system's clock to January 1st, 2002, with no way to change it to the correct time.
Honda and Acura car owners reported that the Y2K22 bug affected almost all older cars, including Honda Pilot, Odyssey, CRV, Ridgeline, Odyssey and Acura MDX, RDX, CSX, and TL models.
A vulnerability was found in Teslamate, allowing attackers to open doors of Tesla vehicles, start keyless driving, and interfere with vehicle operation en route.
This occurs because an attacker can leverage Grafana login access to obtain a token for Tesla API calls.
Polish developer Michał Gapiński shared a look at CarPlay running on his Tesla Model 3 contrary to the fact that Tesla doesn’t support CarPlay and writes its own software for its infotainment system.
The ability to operate CarPlay came with limited functionality, including being run by an in-car Raspberry Pi running a custom build of Android OS.
In addition, Gapiński had to use the Raspberry Pi’s mouse for navigation in place of the touchscreen.
Three stolen Kias from one family in less than a week.
The issue was with base model Kia and Hyundais that use a physical key to start the car.
The cars are missing an anti-theft device so that they can be started without the key.
In three weeks, there were just over 400 reported cars stolen in the city of Columbus.
Of those, 45 reported stolen Kias, and 68 reported stolen Hyundais.
Kia said they were fixing the issue with all new vehicles, but Columbus police said there is a way to protect your car from thieves.
A script published on Github by a security researcher ‘d-Rickyy-b’, enables controlling functions of Ford vehicles via FordPass API.
The script’s features enable controlling the vehicle locking functions and engine ignition.
Experts urged motorists to keep their keys in empty drinks cans or even the microwave after a locked BMW was stolen without obtaining the key.
According to the police, thieves were able to gain access to vehicles by redirecting the wireless signal from a car’s key fob.

The police added that motor vehicles were extremely expensive, and as such owners should take the same precautions as they do with home security and suggested motorists use a blocking pouch also called a Faraday pouch, which is lined with metallic material, to help block the wireless signal from your key fob.

According to the Peel Region Commercial Auto Crime Bureau, crooks could steal a fob signal to get into one's car.
Once they're in, they disable the alarm system.
In some vehicles, that can be done with a screwdriver or a rod to deactivate the horn.
After that, they plug into the vehicle's onboard diagnostic port under the steering column.
Then, use software, which is available online, to program a blank fob to start your car.
Unlike using a wireless relay attack, thieves use a device to scan the signal from your keyless fob sitting inside the house.
The thieves create a cloned fob that lets them get in your car and start it.

According to the police, there were various methods of stealing keyless cars, ranging from hacking the onboard computer or intercepting the key signal to just breaking into a house and stealing the car key.
A hacker modified the firmware of an Electronic Power Steering ( EPS) ECU in a 2010 Volkswagen Golf Mk6.
The hacker tried to extract the firmware over the CAN bus but failed.
However, this resulted in some knowledge on how to brute-force the authentication and enter a password-protected diagnostics mode.
Then, he described how he found a Volkswagen upgrade file and decrypted it.
Finally, he loaded the binary code into Ghidra and made initial guesses at this unknown microcontroller’s architecture and memory map.
The police alleged suspects forced open a driver’s door, obtained access to the vehicle’s On-Board Diagnostic Port, and then used that device to program a new key fob.
As a result, police recovered 217 cars valued at about $11.1 million.

A Hacker who didn’t like how Tesla Model 3 and Model Y have all information displayed on a center console instead of a more traditional dash cluster decided to connect together a dash cluster of his own, calling it the CANdash.
The CANdash worked in a simple fashion, snooping the Tesla’s CAN bus for all the information relevant to the vehicle’s operation.

It was capable of displaying everything from speed to the remaining range in the battery, while also allowing the user to keep an eye on things like coolant temperatures and whether the Tesla Autopilot system was available.
The build relies on a CANserver, an ESP32-based device specifically built for hooking up to the CAN bus on Tesla vehicles and sharing the data externally.
The data can then be piped wirelessly to an Android phone running CANdash to display all the desired information.
By using an aftermarket dash clip or a 3D printed custom mount, the phone can then be placed behind the steering wheel to display data in the usual location.
As an experiment, a CEO of a Canadian-based company called Ingenext hacked an electric vehicle and removed its speed limitations.
As a result, the vehicle reached a top speed of 216 mph.
Ingenext's vehicle included bigger brakes and higher performance tires, the modifications were done mostly for safety reasons.
Accordingly, a regular car might have burnt up its tires and wouldn’t be able to perform a safe halt if it had reached such high speeds.

Seven vulnerabilities were found in EVlink City EVC1S22P4 / EVC1S7P4, EVlink Parking EVW2 / EVF2 / EVP2PE, and EVlink Smart Wallbox EVB1A. Among the potential impacts of the vulnerabilities, were allowing remote attackers to impersonate the user who manages the charging station or carry out actions on their behalf when crafted malicious parameters are submitted to the charging station web server and or impersonate the user or carry out actions on their behalf when crafted malicious parameters are submitted in POST requests sent to the charging station web server.
A hacker claimed he had found flaws in a piece of third-party software used by several Tesla vehicle owners.

David Colombo, a self-described information technology security specialist, claimed that he had found flaws in software that allowed him to unlock doors, open windows, start cars without keys, and disable their security systems.

The number of car thefts in Ontario, Canada has increased by nearly 45% since 2021.
According to Toronto police, most stolen vehicles are with keyless ignitions or push-to-start models.
The three types of keyless vehicles most commonly stolen in Ontario were of the Lexus RX, Honda CR-V, and Honda Civic series.
A total of eight Ford fiestas were stolen via keyless entry between September 7th to 20th, 2022.
According to the Greater Manchester Police, the keyless cars were unlocked by short-range radio waves emitted from a keyless fob.
A vulnerability known as CVE-2022-42430, impacting Tesla model 3, was detected by security researchers.
The affected vehicle part is unknown.
By exploiting it, an attacker can execute code and gain root privileges to the affected vehicles.
Upgrading to the latest version of Model 3, 2022.28 eliminates this vulnerability
Hackers in France figured out how to steal Peugeot, Lexus and Toyota vehicles in less than a minute, using a modified JBL bluetooth speaker to break into the vehicles.
The discovery was made accidentally by Paris police authorities during an arrest of two suspected car hackers.
The search for a stolen Peugeot 2008 revealed a JBL bluetooth speaker containing a quick start key that enabled the hackers to start the vehicle.
The device can be found on the dark web and is marketed for €5,000.
Several keyless entry pickup trucks were stolen in Port Hope and Lindsay, Ontario, Canada.
Police in Ontario believed that the thieves used relay attacks on the owners' keyless fobs to steal the vehicles.
Among the stolen trucks were a 2022 Dodge Rebel 1500, a 2022 Dodge Ram Longhorn, and a 2021 Dodge Ram.
Security researchers found a vulnerability in SiriusXM, a 3rd party services-provider that powers telematics and infotainment systems for connected vehicles.
OEMs typically use SiriusXM services to provide in-vehicle remote functionality.

A critical zero-day vulnerability impacting all versions of Linux released in the last nine years was discovered by security researchers.
The vulnerability allows attackers to gain root access to servers running Samba, a popular open-source implementation of the SMB protocol.
The flaw can be exploited remotely and does not require authentication, making it particularly dangerous.
Police were trying to track down a high-performance car worth tens of thousands of pounds snatched from outside its Wigan owner's home in the UK.

CCTV footage showed a man hacking into the vehicle without using a physical key to open the doors.

According to the police, the thief hacked the vehicle's central locking system.
Criminals have been exploiting technology to get into cars and drive them away without using a physical key fob in Cheshire, UK.
The local police claimed that keyless car theft, or relay theft, a method in which a device is used to manipulate a car into thinking the key is close by has seen a spike in use.

According to the police, the thieves needed to be within a few meters of your car key to capture the signal, even if it’s inside the driver’s house, meaning that even if the vehicle and home are secure, thieves can still unlock, start and steal your car.
As such, in light of a rise in Range Rover vehicles thefts in Cheshire, the local police have issued the following safety tips to help drivers protect their vehicles.
Numerous Mazda drivers in and around Seattle, USA, discovered they could no longer change the radio station or use other functionalities after listening to the local NPR station KUOW.
The issue affected owners of various Mazda vehicles with model years ranging from 2014 to 2017 that were tuned in to the station.

A bug in the car’s infotainment software crashed after trying to load an image file that was missing an extension, and the infotainment software could not decode it and had no process for handling it.
The solution involves replacing the CMU, the hardware computer component of the infotainment system.

Siemens, an automotive software and systems provider, informed customers about more than 100 vulnerabilities affecting its products, including over 90 security flaws introduced by the use of third-party components.
Three advisories were marked critical and eight were high severity across Mendix, COMOS, Simcenter, SIMOTICS, SINEC, RUGGEDCOM, and SINUMERIK products.
Five of Siemens’ March 2022 Patch Tuesday advisories cover vulnerabilities affecting third-party components.
One of them described the impact on SINEC INS of 71 security holes affecting components such as Node.js, cURL, SQLite, CivetWeb, and BIND.
Another advisory described over a dozen vulnerabilities affecting COMOS, specifically the Drawings SDK used by the product.

Researchers at Duke University demonstrated the first attack strategy that can fool industry-standard autonomous vehicle sensors into believing nearby objects are closer ( or further) than they appear without being detected.
The researchers suggested that adding optical 3D capabilities or the ability to share data with nearby cars may be necessary to fully protect autonomous cars from attacks.
The new attack strategy worked by shooting a laser gun into a car’s LIDAR sensor to add false data points to its perception.
The research was conducted under the assumption that these data points were wildly out of place with what a car’s camera was seeing.
In addition, previous research has shown that the system could recognize the attack.
However, the new research from showed that 3D LIDAR data points carefully placed within a certain area of a camera’s 2D field of view can fool the system.

A vulnerability was found in NVIDIA chip series, among which was the Jetson AGX Xavier™ series, a chip used in the automotive industry, where an error in the IOMMU configuration may allow an unprivileged attacker with physical access to the board direct read or write access to the entire system address space through the PCI bus.
Such an attack could result in denial of service, code execution, escalation of privileges, and impact on data integrity and confidentiality.
The scope impact may extend to other components.
Police are warning car owners to be vigilant after another keyless theft in the Ardglena Grove area of Dungannon.
A white Hyundai Tucson parked in the driveway at a property in the area was stolen in mid-March.
The vehicle was locked, and the owner still had both keys.
In January, CCTV footage of two men attempting to steal a car in the Bush area of Dungannon was posted online by the vehicle’s owner.
Their attempt was foiled, as the owner had stored the keys in a signal-blocking ( Faraday) pouch.

Four Ram 1500s were recently stolen from the Sterling Heights Stellantis Assembly Plant in Michigan, one of them being a high-performance Ram 1500 TRX.
The thieves relied on its high performance to smash through the front gate and make their escape, just one week after a similar incident involving the same vehicle model.
These are in addition to five Ram trucks being stolen from a lot in Shelby Township, while three Dodge Charger Hellcat Widebody models were taken from a lot in Auburn Hills on March 3rd.
The month before, a Jeep Grand Cherokee Trackhawk and Dodge Challenger Hellcat were stolen from the Jefferson North Assembly Plant in Detroit.

The officers received five reports of keyless Range Rover thefts in the Alderley Edge and Wilmslow areas.
Two of the vehicles have since been recovered in the Greater Manchester area.

According to the police, in the series of thefts, it was confirmed that most of the vehicles were stolen without the need for a physical key, commonly referred to as keyless thefts or relay thefts, where offenders can use devices that copy the signal of the typical key to gain access to the vehicle and start the ignition.
A group of cybersecurity researchers published a proof of concept for a vulnerability in Honda’s remote keyless system.
The researchers posted videos demonstrating the use of a radio transceiver to lock, unlock, and remote start a 10th generation ( 2016-2021) Honda Civic.
The videos served as proof of the capacity for hackers to exploit a vulnerability in Honda’s remote keyless system.
The vulnerability was listed in the National Vulnerability Database ( NVD) as CVE-2022-27254.
Honda’s remote keyless system sends the same radio frequency ( RF) code for each request, rather than employing a rolling code technique that changes the code after every request.

As a result, Hondas and Acuras were open to replay Man-in-the-Middle ( MitM) attacks, where a nearby attacker intercepts the RF codes sent by the remote keyless system and later uses them to lock, unlock, or remote start the car.
A vulnerability was found in automotive grade Linux Kooky Koi 11.0.0, 11.0.1, 11.0.2, 11.0.3, 11.0.4, and 11.0.5.
The vulnerability can be affected by Incorrect Access Control in usr/bin/afb-daemon.
To exploit the vulnerability, an attacker should send a well-crafted HTTP ( or WebSocket) request to the socket listened by the afb-daemon process.
No credentials nor user interactions are required.

A group of academics from the University of Oxford and Armasuisse S+T disclosed details of a new attack technique against the popular Combined Charging System ( CCS) that could potentially disrupt the ability to charge electric vehicles at scale.

Called Brokenwire, the method interferes with the control communications that transpire between the vehicle and charger to wirelessly abort the charging sessions from a distance of as far as 47m (151ft).

The researchers explained that while it may only be an inconvenience for individuals, interrupting the charging process of critical vehicles, such as electric ambulances, could have life-threatening consequences.

The researchers added that Brokenwire had immediate implications for many of the 12 million battery EVs estimated to be on the roads worldwide — and profound effects on the new wave of electrification for vehicle fleets, both for private enterprise and for crucial public services.

According to a Marketplace investigation, cars stolen from Ontario and Quebec in Canada were openly advertised and sold in West African countries, including Nigeria and Ghana, which also found thieves are targeting vehicles with push-to-start ignitions.

According to experts, OEMs prioritize convenience over security with push-to-start ignitions allowing thieves to quickly and easily steal vehicles to ship overseas, where demand for Canadian cars is high because of their reliability and the availability of parts, and the consequences for thieves are low.
To steal the vehicles, thieves use a relay attack, in which a device is used to capture the signal of a car key fob inside a house and then amplified to open car doors.
However, experts claimed that there was a cheaper and easier solution thieves have been turning to lock picks.

Once inside the car, thieves typically plug a crucial programmer, available for under $1,000 online, into the car’s On-Board Diagnostics ( OBD) port, usually located under the steering wheel, where mechanics can plug in a diagnostic tool the car’s computer.
Thieves can program a blank key fob to match the vehicle using this port.
It can be done on nearly any vehicle with push-to-start ignition, and vehicles with physical keys require a separate tool to clone the key.

A high vulnerability ( CVE-2022-28062) was found in a car rental management system containing an arbitrary file upload vulnerability via the Add Car component which allows attackers to upload a webshell and execute arbitrary code.
Security research revealed vulnerabilities in the ALAC format of Qualcomm chipsets, which are also used in automotive infotainment systems.
By exploiting these vulnerabilities, threat actors could remotely listen to audio conversations and view media on affected devices.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by Check Point, and can be exploitable through remote code execution attacks on mobile devices.
In addition, an unprivileged Android app could exploit the vulnerabilities to escalate its privileges and access user data.
The Nigerian Communications Commission ( NCC) warned of an ongoing cyber-vulnerability that allowed a nearby hacker to unlock vehicles, start their engines wirelessly and make away with cars.

In a statement, the NCC said that the fact that car remotes were categorized short-range devices that make use of radio frequency ( RF) to lock and unlock cars informed the need for the Commission to alert the general public of this emergent danger, where hackers take advantage to unlock and start a compromised car.

It was reported that the vulnerability was a Man-in-the-Middle ( MitM) attack or, more specifically, a replay attack in which an attacker intercepts the RF signals normally sent from a remote key fob to the car, manipulates these signals, and re-sends them later to unlock the car at will.

Three vulnerabilities were found in the oretnom23 automotive shop management system v1.0, allowing attackers to change the admin password, dump all database credentials and gain admin access and view internal data.
The vulnerabilities exploited XSS injection, blind SQL Injection Vulnerability, and Broken Access Control.

Experts have seen a rise in charging station hacking incidents in the past few months, including incidents where hackers would load ransomware onto chargers to slow them down or stop functionality altogether.
In addition, it was reported that hackers could also lock users out of their user profiles until they pay a ransom fee, or hack into the chargers themselves to save on charging fees.
Hackers discovered a new attack vector in a Chinese OEM vehicle, which allowed them to conduct unapproved software upgrades to their vehicles.
Despite being outside of the approved update region, the systems can be accessed remotely via OTA updates or physically via the OBD port.
In some models, the ability to upgrade these systems at the push of a button extended beyond simple features, such as engine power and safety features.
Pirated installations raise concerns regarding malfunctions in-vehicle systems, including active safety systems.
Russian soldiers remotely disabled and stole 27 agricultural vehicles, worth $5 million USD, including combine harvesters and tractors from a John Deere dealership in Melitopol, Ukraine.
The vehicles were equipped with GPS and geofencing ( a virtual perimeter) and their journey could be tracked.
Anti-theft devices installed on the stolen vehicles, had been remotely activated to lock the stolen combine harvesters and prevent them from working.

A vulnerability ( CVE-2022-29318) was found in a car rental management system, in which an arbitrary file could be uploaded in the New Entry module of Car Rental Management System v1.0 which would allow attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted PHP file.
The Ottawa Police Service ( OPS) warned residents about an increase in car thefts where the suspects mainly targeted newer models of the Honda CRV.
There have been 21 Honda CRVs stolen in two weeks.
Although the Honda CRV was reported the most, there were still other types of vehicles being stolen.
The thieves have been targeting models with a proximity key, the kind of key you use for a push-button start.
Some of the models taken included newer models of the Dodge Durango, Jeep Grand Cherokee, Toyota Highlander, Lexus RX, and particular Ford F-Series trucks.

The police service noted a shift in trends regarding vehicle thefts and saw a sudden spike in CRV thefts from owner driveways and more vehicles taken from car dealerships outside their hours of operation.
The OPS added that over 230 cars were reported stolen by the end of May 2022, compared to half during the same time frame in 2021.

The OPS said vehicle thefts usually happened in one of two ways: The driver-side door was mechanically breached, at which point thieves accessed the vehicle’s engine control module ( ECM) port to reprogram a new key.
This was the most common type of vehicle theft, and it is not deterred by using a radio frequency shield ( known as a faraday bag or box.)
The signal amplification relay attack ( SARA) was not a common technique in Ottawa.
However, police continued to raise public awareness about this means where thieves use an amplification device to amplify the signal emanating from the key fob inside the house.
That signal would then be relayed to the car, which unlocks the vehicle and allows it to be started.
This type of theft would be deterred by using a radio frequency shield ( the faraday bag or box.)
Three thieves used a software-based hacking device to steal over 40 vehicles in New Delhi.
Each targeted car was stolen within two to three minutes as attackers tricked their systems into accepting new keys.
New Delhi police arrested three men owning discovered the crew’s hi-tech tools, including scanners and GPS jamming devices.
The team was reported to have used the relay method to unlock and then steal the cars.
With access granted, blank keys could be programmed to a vehicle to make it appear that nothing is wrong with it.
The thieves stole vehicles such as Maruti Suzuki Brezza, Hyundai Venue, Maruti Suzuki Swift, and Hyundai Creta.
The insurance crime bureau warned of an increase in car thefts by criminal syndicates using a method known as relay attacks.
Relay attacks target new-generation cars that have keyless entry and ignition technology.
Another option was to place the key fob in a signal blocking wallet or sheath.
The criminals intercept the signals sent by the key fob while looking for the linked car, which allows them to open the car and steal whatever is inside, or even the vehicle itself.

The bureau said it had recently seen an increase in the theft of newer model sports utility vehicles ( SUVs) with keyless entry and ignition technology, with criminal syndicates using relay attacks to steal these vehicles.
In essence, a car’s key fob is constantly transmitting signals looking for the linked vehicle.
The signal allows the driver to gain keyless entry and operate the car when the key is in close proximity to it.
By amplifying the signal, the perpetrators tap into the active emission of the key fob signal, allowing them to open and drive off with the vehicle.
An individual possessing the amplifying device walked close to the unsuspecting owner when they exited and left the car.
At the same time, an accomplice at the vehicle gained access and drove off with it.
The bureau said that the best protection against relay attacks was to deactivate the key fob when exiting the car immediately and while still next to it.
The keyless entry systems are easy to break due to vulnerabilities of the radio signals used to unlock the doors.
Ford developed a solution to prevent the most common theft method, called the key fob relay attack.
In addition, to avoid this kind of man-in-the-middle attack, it’s best to have a system that works at a very close distance.
Newer vehicles use NFC to open and start, which is far more secure than a radio signal that can be sniffed further away.

The keyless entry system, which added convenience to unlocking and starting a vehicle since there’s no need to use a physical key anymore, was vulnerable to attacks that led to many car thefts worldwide, as thieves had discovered that too soon stealing a car became very easy.
Ford found a solution and filed a patent to protect it.
Called system for preventing vehicle key fob relay attacks, the patent describes a new authentication system that allows the car to know whether the original key is near the vehicle or not.
According to the patent filed on October 29, 2020, and published on May 5, 2022, the authentication system can obtain historical data, including the time and location of the key fob.
Thus it can determine if the person trying to unlock the car is the owner or another person.
For instance, since the car knows that the key moved away when the owner left the vehicle, it will not respond to a signal that suddenly appears in its vicinity.
There is still a place for improvement, as the spoofing devices can emulate the key even in approaching the vehicle.
Still, it’s progress in finding a solution to a significant attack method used by thieves, impacting the automotive industry.
A team of hackers with offensive security company Synacktiv found two unique bugs in the Tesla Model 3 Infotainment System.

Car thieves turned to a two-person system that, with the help of technology, allows them to pop the locks on cars with keyless entry and then, if the vehicle has a keyless start, drive off.

A citizen of South Austin, Texas, said his neighborhood had been hit by thieves using what are known as relay devices to get into locked vehicles, with at least three people that were roaming around a particular street.
Two cars were stolen in one night.
The method the thieves used was that one would go to the front door of an unsuspecting house because many people store key fobs near the front door.
They will capture and amplify the signal from the fob just inside the door.
Meanwhile, the second thief will wait by the car, holding a second hacking device near the car door.
The vehicle, engineered to do as the key fob says, opens the door, allowing the thieves to either take the car’s content or, in some cases, the vehicle itself.
The Insurance Crime Bureau has warned of an increase in car thefts by criminal syndicates using a method known as a relay attack.
This device targets new-generation cars that have keyless entry and ignition technology.
It’s different from the known signal-jamming device, which prevents the vehicle from locking so criminals can access it.
The device gives criminals access to the car to copy the signal — meaning they can unlock and start the car and drive away.

The device, examples of which police have confiscated, intercepts the signals sent by the key fob while looking for the linked car, allowing criminals to open it and steal the contents or even the vehicle itself.
A new research paper showing a vulnerability with Bluetooth Low Energy ( BLE) was used to single out Tesla, potentially resulting in remotely unlocking vehicles.

Tesla announced they conducted the world’s first link-layer relay attack on Bluetooth Low Energy ( BLE), the standard protocol used for sharing data between devices that companies have adopted for proximity authentication to unlock millions of vehicles, residential smart locks, commercial building access control systems, smartphones, smartwatches, laptops and more.
As they wrote, this was a specific exploit related to BLE, and it affected virtually every device that uses the protocol.
Still, the reason Tesla was being singled out was that they demonstrated the vulnerability of Tesla vehicles.
An attacker can unlock, start, and drive a car in cars with automotive keyless entry.

A security researcher showed how the feature could be exploited to steal cars by manipulating the state where drivers who used their Tesla NFC key card to unlock their vehicles had to place the card on the center console to begin driving.
The feature was introduced to the world In 2021 when Tesla issued an update that made its vehicles easier to start after being unlocked with their NFC key cards.

The hacker noticed that not only did the feature allow the car to automatically start within 130 seconds of being unlocked with the NFC card, but it also put the car in a state to accept entirely new keys, with no authentication required and zero indication given by the in-car display.

The hacker explained that authorization given in the 130-second interval was too general, not only for driving, and added that the timer was introduced by Tesla to make using the NFC card as a primary means of using the car more convenient.
Users of Bluetooth devices were negatively impacted by a phenomenon called bluejacking.
Among the devices targeted by hackers are Tesla vehicles, which are Bluetooth enabled.
Generally, bluejacking involves one Bluetooth device hijacking another one and sending spam advertising or other types of unsolicited messages.
Hackers can exploit a Bluetooth technology vulnerabilities to bluejack devices within 10 to 30 feet of the target.
Crowded public places are the most common places where bluejacking attacks occur.
A major concern about bluejacking is that hackers are able to unlock and lock smart locks and car doors.

Researchers discovered a key fob vulnerability affecting major Japanese OEM’s car models from 2012 to 2022, which they named Rolling-PWN.
The researchers worked under the assumption that modern vehicles are often equipped with remote keyless entry ( RKE) systems that allow vehicles to be unlocked or started remotely.
Their research goal was to evaluate the resistance of a modern RKE system.
Furthermore, although the research was primarily focused on Japanese OEM vehicles, the researchers discovered that the vulnerability also applied to other global OEMs.
According to the researchers, a local dealer would have to recall a vehicle to fix the Rolling-PWN bug.
In any case, OTA updates of the vulnerable firmware would be the recommended mitigation strategy.
BMW recently announced it will charge car owners with a subscription fee to use heated seats, leveraging capabilities and hardware already installed in vehicles.

A hacker could compromise an MV720 device to track or immobilize the vehicle carrying it, collect tracking information, and manipulate data.

Teenagers used small handheld radios to wirelessly open the doors to Tesla charging ports, using a device called Flipper Zero.

Local law enforcement believe attackers used keyless relay devices to access the vehicles.
